evt-hallstatt-origins: A richly worked Hallstatt-era gold neck-ring from Uttendorf, Austria — the kind of treasure these Iron Age chieftains were rich enough to take into the grave
evt-hallstatt-salt-mines: A Bronze Age timber staircase deep in the Hallstatt salt mine, built around 1344 BCE — the salty air preserved it intact for over three thousand years
evt-hallstatt-dagger-type: Hallstatt-type iron swords from Wels, Austria — long blades made for cutting down from horseback, the left one keeping its ornate decorated pommel
evt-celtic-wine-trade: A bronze cross-handled wine bowl from Hallstatt — the elaborate drinking gear that turned imported Mediterranean wine into the centerpiece of a chieftain's feast
evt-heuneburg: The reconstructed Heuneburg on the upper Danube, its buildings backed by the white mudbrick wall its rulers copied straight from the Greek world around 600 BCE
evt-hallstatt-elite-burials: A cutaway model of a Hallstatt chieftain's grave — a wooden chamber packed with goods, sealed under a huge earthen mound ringed with stone
evt-hochdorf-burial: The reconstructed Hochdorf chieftain's grave near Stuttgart — the dead man laid out on a bronze couch beside a four-wheeled wagon loaded with bronze dishes for the afterlife
evt-vix-burial: The Vix krater, over five feet tall and the largest bronze vessel to survive from antiquity — Greek-made, hauled over the Alps, and buried with a Celtic woman around 500 BCE
evt-celtic-expansion-iberia: A Celtiberian antenna-hilted iron sword — the short, double-edged blade so effective that Rome copied it wholesale as the gladius hispaniensis
evt-golasecca-culture: A decorated bronze situla from a Golasecca grave — the kind of fine metalwork these Alpine middlemen traded between the Mediterranean and the Celtic north
evt-lepontic-inscriptions: The Prestino stone near Como, carved with a line of Lepontic — the oldest surviving Celtic writing, in an alphabet borrowed from the Etruscans
evt-amber-trade: Iron Age amber beads strung with bronze spirals — Baltic amber, warm and glowing, worked into the jewelry that traveled the whole length of Europe
evt-pj-odai-yamamoto: Potsherds from the Ōdai Yamamoto I site in Aomori, northern Japan — among the oldest pottery in the world, dated to roughly 14,500 BCE
evt-norse-longhouse: Reconstructed Viking chieftain's longhouse at the Lofotr Viking Museum, Vestvågøy, Norway
evt-eridu-temple: Ruins of the ancient Sumerian ziggurat at Eridu, southern Iraq, with stamped bricks from King Ur-Nammu's construction
evt-inanna-worship: The goddess Inanna (Ishtar) depicted on an Akkadian cylinder seal, shown with wings and weapons as the goddess of love and war
evt-wheel-invention: Detail of the Standard of Ur (c. 2600 BCE) showing Sumerian war carts on solid wooden wheels — the earliest depictions of the wheel in use.
evt-cylinder-seal: Cylinder seal and its clay impression showing the king-priest feeding the sacred herd, Uruk period, c. 3200 BCE
evt-cuneiform-invention: A proto-cuneiform tablet from the Oriental Institute Museum, roughly 3100 BCE — an early step from pictographic tokens to wedge-shaped writing.
evt-beer-brewing: The Alulu Beer Receipt (c. 2050 BCE), a Sumerian cuneiform tablet recording a delivery of the finest beer — among the oldest written beer records.
evt-silk-road-precursor: Raw lapis lazuli stone with golden pyrite inclusions, sourced from Afghanistan
evt-elamite-rivalry: Map showing the extent of ancient Elam in relation to Mesopotamia
evt-gilgamesh-person: The Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, a cuneiform fragment of the Epic of Gilgamesh — one of the world's oldest surviving works of literature.
evt-royal-tombs-ur: Black-and-white photograph of the Royal Cemetery of Ur excavations
evt-early-dynastic-wars: The Stele of the Vultures in the Louvre Museum, commemorating a Sumerian military victory
evt-sumerian-trade-networks: Map of the ancient Near East in the 3rd millennium BCE, showing Sumerian maritime trade routes and partner cities
evt-eannatum: Fragment of the Stele of the Vultures showing King Eannatum of Lagash leading troops, Louvre Museum
evt-shekel-weight: Electrum stater coin from Carthage, c. 310–290 BCE, showing the head of Tanit
evt-sumerian-astronomy: The MUL.APIN astronomical tablet at the British Museum — a compilation of star lists, calendar rules, and planetary observations going back to Sumerian times.
evt-lugalzagesi: Akkadian victory stele from the era of Lugal-zage-si, showing a prisoner exiting a cage, c. 2300 BCE, Louvre Museum
evt-sargon-akkad: Bronze head believed to represent an Akkadian king, possibly Sargon or Naram-Sin, Iraq Museum, Baghdad
evt-enheduanna: Calcite disk depicting Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad, history's first known author
evt-naram-sin: Victory Stele of Naram-Sin showing the Akkadian king ascending a mountain over fallen enemies, Louvre Museum
evt-gudea-lagash: Diorite statue of Gudea of Lagash, dedicated to the god Ningishzida, c. 2120 BCE
evt-ur-nammu: Stone carving depicting King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur
evt-code-ur-nammu: Clay tablet fragment bearing the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest surviving law code, Istanbul Archaeological Museum
evt-ziggurat-ur: Remains of the Great Ziggurat of Ur in southern Iraq, originally built c. 2100 BCE
evt-epic-gilgamesh-written: The Flood Tablet (Tablet 11 of the Epic of Gilgamesh), Neo-Assyrian clay tablet from the Library of Ashurbanipal, British Museum
evt-sumerian-king-list: The Weld-Blundell Prism, a four-sided clay prism inscribed with the Sumerian King List
evt-shulgi: Line drawing of a cylinder seal impression attributed to King Shulgi of Ur
evt-mari-kingdom: Ruins of a ziggurat near the royal palace at Mari, Syria
evt-babylonian-mathematics: Clay tablet YBC 7289 from the Yale Babylonian Collection showing a square with diagonal and sexagesimal calculations
evt-plimpton-322: Plimpton 322, a Babylonian clay tablet listing Pythagorean triples, c. 1800 BCE
evt-hammurabi: Votive monument dedicated to Hammurabi, king of Babylon, British Museum
evt-code-hammurabi: Upper portion of the Code of Hammurabi stele showing the king receiving authority from the god Shamash, Louvre Museum
evt-babylon-marduk: The head of a mušḫuššu, Marduk's serpent-dragon, from Babylon — the symbol of the god who rose to supremacy over the Mesopotamian pantheon.
evt-atra-hasis: A Met Museum cuneiform tablet of the Atra-Hasis, the Babylonian flood myth where the gods send a deluge to thin an overpopulated world.
evt-hittite-sack-babylon: "The Fall of Babylon" — mezzotint by John Martin, 1831, depicting Cyrus the Great defeating the Chaldean army
evt-mitanni-kingdom: Map of the Mitanni kingdom at its greatest extent, showing major cities and archaeological sites
evt-amarna-letters: Five Amarna Letters on display at the British Museum — diplomatic correspondence between Egyptian pharaohs and Near Eastern rulers
evt-tukulti-ninurta: Stone base with cuneiform inscription showing Tukulti-Ninurta I standing and kneeling before a divine symbol, 13th century BCE
evt-assyrian-conquest-babylon: The Statue of Marduk depicted on a 9th-century BCE cylinder seal — Assyrian conquerors carried this sacred statue from Babylon as a trophy of war
evt-bronze-age-collapse: Map showing migrations, invasions, and destructions during the Bronze Age Collapse, c. 1200 BCE
evt-nebuchadnezzar-i: Kudurru (boundary stone) from the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I, recording a land grant and tax exemption, 12th century BCE
evt-tiglath-pileser-i: Stone relief depicting Tiglath-Pileser I, king of Assyria
evt-enuma-elish: The Ashmolean's Enuma Elish tablet (AN1926.373) — the Babylonian creation epic that elevated Marduk to king of the gods.
evt-mul-apin: The MUL.APIN tablet — clay tablet with two columns of astronomical text listing star catalogues, British Museum
evt-new-year-festival: Modern Assyrian community celebrating the Akitu (New Year) festival, 2019
evt-ashurnasirpal-ii: Stone relief showing King Ashurnasirpal II meeting a high official during a review of soldiers and prisoners
evt-nimrud: Pair of lamassu (winged human-headed bulls) guarding the entrance to Ashurnasirpal's palace at Nimrud
evt-shalmaneser-iii: Stone relief detail depicting King Shalmaneser III of Assyria
evt-battle-qarqar: The Kurkh Stela of Shalmaneser III, recording the Battle of Qarqar in 853 BCE
evt-babylonian-eclipse: Babylonian clay tablet recording astronomical observations, British Museum
evt-tiglath-pileser-iii: Gypsum wall panel relief of King Tiglath-Pileser III wearing royal robes with a full beard and ceremonial mace
evt-tiglath-pileser-conquests: Map showing Assyrian deportation routes — Tiglath-Pileser III systematized mass population transfers as imperial policy
evt-fall-of-israel: Panel from the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III showing Israelite delegates bearing tribute to the Assyrian king, British Museum
evt-sennacherib: Cast of a rock relief of King Sennacherib from the mountain of Cudi Dağı, near Cizre, Turkey
evt-sennacherib-jerusalem: Remnants of the Broad Wall in Jerusalem, built by King Hezekiah in preparation for Sennacherib's siege
evt-babylonian-zodiac: 19th-century engraving of an Assyrian astronomical scene related to celestial observation
evt-nineveh-capital: The reconstructed Mashki Gate at the ancient site of Nineveh, Iraq
evt-esarhaddon: Basalt victory stele of King Esarhaddon holding ropes attached to conquered rulers, Pergamon Museum, Berlin
evt-assyrian-conquest-egypt: Map of the Neo-Assyrian Empire at its greatest territorial extent, 824–671 BCE
evt-ashurbanipal: Stone relief of King Ashurbanipal hunting a lion from horseback, British Museum
evt-library-nineveh: Cuneiform tablets from the Library of Ashurbanipal on display at the British Museum
evt-destruction-elam: Assyrian relief depicting the destruction of the Elamite city of Hamanu, c. 645–635 BCE
evt-battle-carchemish: Illustration of the Battle of Carchemish from Hutchinson's History of the Nations, 1915
evt-nebuchadnezzar-ii: Artist's reconstruction of the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II
evt-nebuchadnezzar-ii-person: Artist's reconstruction of the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II
evt-hanging-gardens: 19th-century artist's imagining of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, inspired by early archaeological excavations
evt-chaldean-dynasty: Map of Babylonia during the Chaldean period, showing the centers of astronomical observation and major cities
evt-etemenanki: Architectural reconstruction drawing of the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon
evt-mesopotamia-destruction-jerusalem: 19th-century Bible illustration depicting the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylonian forces
evt-ishtar-gate: Reconstructed Ishtar Gate of Babylon, covered in blue-glazed bricks with relief figures of bulls and dragons, Pergamon Museum, Berlin
evt-nabonidus: Detail of a stele showing King Nabonidus in traditional Babylonian royal dress, holding symbols of authority
evt-fall-babylon-persia: "The Fall of Babylon" — mezzotint by John Martin, 1831, depicting the Persian conquest
evt-cyrus-cylinder: The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay barrel inscribed with a declaration by Cyrus the Great after his conquest of Babylon, British Museum
evt-mehrgarh-settlement: Archaeological ruins of Mehrgarh, one of the earliest Neolithic farming villages in South Asia, Balochistan, Pakistan
evt-ravi-phase-harappa: Map of early Harappan sites during the Ravi and Hakra phases, showing the earliest settlements in the Indus region
evt-kot-diji-founded: View of Kot Diji Fort from the town below, Sindh, Pakistan
evt-kalibangan-plowed-field: The western mound (citadel) at the ruins of Kalibangan, Rajasthan, India
evt-early-indus-script: Clay impression of an Indus Valley seal showing five characters of the undeciphered Indus script
evt-kot-diji-burned: Kot Diji Fort, Sindh, Pakistan — the site shows evidence of a major fire destruction layer
evt-mature-harappan-begins: Map of the Indus Valley Civilization during the Mature Harappan phase, 2600–1900 BCE
evt-mohenjo-daro-built: View of the Buddhist-era stupa mound at Mohenjo-daro, with the ancient city ruins in the foreground
evt-dholavira-built: Layout plan of Dholavira showing the city's distinctive three-part division: citadel, middle town, and lower town
evt-rakhigarhi: Excavation site at Rakhigarhi, the largest known Harappan settlement, Haryana, India
evt-urban-planning: The excavated grid layout at Lothal — every major Harappan city was built to a rectilinear plan with streets running on cardinal directions.
evt-harappa-city: The mounds of Harappa in Pakistani Punjab — the northern anchor city, and the one British railway engineers famously mined for track ballast in 1856.
evt-drainage-system: Covered brick drains at Lothal — Harappan cities built drainage networks more sophisticated than anything in the ancient world until Rome, two thousand years later.
evt-standardized-weights: Cubical chert weights from Mohenjo-daro, now in the Ashmolean — ground to binary ratios (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) and accurate to a tenth of a gram across the entire civilization.
evt-indus-script-seals: Collection of Indus script characters from various seals, showing the range of the still-undeciphered writing system
evt-granaries-harappa: Ruins of the granary and great hall at Harappa — centralized grain storage suggesting organized food distribution
evt-bead-making: Harappan carnelian beads recovered from the Royal Cemetery at Ur in Mesopotamia — the export trade in these beads reached 1,500 miles from their workshops at Chanhu-daro and Lothal.
evt-dancing-girl: The Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, a bronze figurine c. 2300–1750 BCE, one of the most famous Indus Valley artifacts
evt-pashupati-seal: The Pashupati Seal from Mohenjo-daro, depicting a seated figure surrounded by animals, possibly a proto-Shiva deity
evt-mother-goddess: A Mature Harappan terracotta female figurine with elaborate headdress and jewelry — a figurine type found at every major Indus city, usually interpreted as a mother goddess.
evt-cotton-cultivation: A cotton plant in bloom — the Indus Valley was the earliest known center of cotton cultivation
evt-urban-wells: View of the mound at Mohenjo-daro, where public wells were integral to the city's water supply system
evt-harappan-city-councils: Map of the Indus Valley Civilization showing major governance centers during the Mature phase
evt-lothal-founded: The ancient dockyard at Lothal, Gujarat — the world's oldest known dock, connecting the Indus trade network to the Arabian Sea
evt-mesopotamia-trade: Map showing trade connections between the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia, with major routes and trading centers
evt-dilmun-trade: Cuneiform receipt for garments sent by boat to Dilmun (Bahrain), documenting the maritime trade that connected India and Mesopotamia, British Museum
evt-magan-copper-trade: Map of the 3rd millennium BCE Near East showing Magan (Oman), source of copper traded to the Indus Valley
evt-dholavira-signboard: The 'Ten Indus Scripts' signboard discovered near the northern gateway of the Dholavira citadel — the largest known Indus inscription
evt-dholavira-reservoirs: Aerial view of the excavated water reservoir system at Dholavira, Gujarat, India
evt-unicorn-seal: A steatite seal from Mohenjo-daro depicting the mysterious 'unicorn' — a one-horned bovine figure that appears on most Harappan seals, never explained.
evt-ivory-comb: A carved-ivory long die from Mohenjo-daro at the British Museum — one of the gaming pieces that hint at a sophisticated craft industry in worked ivory.
evt-administrative-seals: A group of steatite seals from Harappa at the National Museum, Delhi — pressed into wet clay to mark packages, doors, and administrative records across the civilization.
evt-fire-altars: The western citadel mound at Kalibangan, where fire altars suggesting ritual practices were discovered
evt-burial-practices: A Harappan burial at Rakhigarhi — most people were buried in simple pits with pottery grave goods, no pyramids, no royal tombs, no obvious social hierarchy in death.
evt-fortification-walls: The massive fortification walls at Dholavira in Gujarat — up to 60 feet thick at the base, enclosing a city that survived in the salt desert for nearly 1,200 years.
evt-ruler-measurement: Brick drainage channel at Lothal — the standardized brick sizes reflect the Indus decimal measurement system
evt-animal-veneration: An elephant seal from the Indus Valley at the British Museum — one of many animals that recur on Harappan seals alongside the bull, the tiger, the rhinoceros, and the buffalo.
evt-indus-metallurgy: The Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro — a 4.1-inch bronze figurine cast in lost-wax and dated to around 2500 BCE, the most famous surviving example of Harappan metallurgy.
evt-toy-carts: A Harappan terracotta toy cart — children's toys from Mohenjo-daro that also provide some of the earliest evidence for wheeled vehicles in South Asia.
evt-indus-games: Cubic dice from Mohenjo-daro in the Ashmolean — the Harappans were rolling six-sided dice with dots two thousand years before anyone else we know of.
evt-climate-shift: Global map showing regions affected by the 4.2 kiloyear climate event that contributed to the Indus decline
evt-surkotada: Map of Indus Valley Civilization sites, including Surkotada where controversial horse bone evidence was found
evt-decline-begins: Map of the Mature Harappan phase showing the full extent of the civilization before its decline began
evt-mohenjo-daro-massacre: The stupa mound at Mohenjo-daro — scattered skeletons found here sparked debate about the city's violent end
evt-cemetery-h: Map of Rigvedic-era geography showing the transition zone between late Harappan and early Vedic cultures
evt-deurbanization: Map of the Indus Valley Civilization showing the pattern of urban abandonment during de-urbanization
evt-pirak-settlement: Ruins near the Pirak archaeological site in Balochistan, a bridge settlement between Harappan and later cultures
evt-late-harappan-craft: Cemetery H pottery from a post-urban Harappan burial ground — the distinctive Late Harappan style that appeared as the great cities emptied out.
evt-vedic-period-begins: Map of Early Vedic culture, c. 1700–1100 BCE, showing the geographic shift from Indus centers to the Ganges plain
evt-end-civilization: Map of the full Mature Harappan phase — by 1300 BCE, all of these urban centers had been abandoned
evt-great-bath: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro — a 39-by-23-foot brick-lined tank on the citadel, sealed with bitumen against leaks and fed by its own well.
evt-priest-king: The 'Priest-King' of Mohenjo-daro — a 7.3-inch steatite bust with serene half-closed eyes that may not depict a priest, or a king, or any single person at all.
evt-chanhu-daro: Beads from Chanhu-daro in Sindh — a small Harappan city that specialized in bead and seal manufacturing for export across the civilization.
evt-uruk-city: The excavated mud-brick remains of Uruk at modern Warka in southern Iraq, the first settlement to cross every threshold that defines a city.
evt-irrigation-systems: A Sumerian cuneiform tablet at the Met recording irrigation work — the kind of bureaucratic bookkeeping that kept the canals running.
evt-white-temple-uruk: The remains of the White Temple platform at Uruk — forerunner to the massive stepped ziggurats that would define Mesopotamian sacred architecture.
evt-sexagesimal-system: Plimpton 322, a Babylonian mathematical tablet listing Pythagorean triples in base-60 — evidence that Sumerian math was far more sophisticated than a counting tool.
evt-temple-economy: A Sumerian administrative tablet from Istanbul — the kind of daily ration record that ran the temple economy.
evt-flood-narrative: The Sumerian Flood Story tablet (CBS 10673) at the Penn Museum — a millennium older than the biblical Genesis flood account.
evt-gutian-invasion: A 19th-century illustration of the Gutians sacking a Mesopotamian city — the mountain people whose raids ended the Akkadian Empire.
evt-fall-of-ur: The Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur (Louvre AO 6446), a Sumerian poem mourning the fall of Ur III to the Elamites.
evt-isin-larsa: An Isin-Larsa period cylinder seal — the era when rival Sumerian kings at Isin and Larsa divided the south before Hammurabi's Babylon swallowed them both.
evt-old-assyrian-trade: The excavated Assyrian merchant colony (karum) at Kanesh in central Anatolia — thousands of cuneiform business letters documenting the trade network were found here.
evt-descent-of-inanna: The British Museum's tablet of Ishtar's Descent to the Underworld (K.162) — the Akkadian version of Inanna's katabasis through seven gates.
evt-kassite-dynasty: A kudurru — a Kassite-period boundary stone carved with divine symbols, the signature legal document of the dynasty that ruled Babylon for over 400 years.
evt-aramean-migrations: Sculptural orthostats from the Aramaean palace at Tell Halaf in Syria (c. 9th century BCE) — the wave of migrants whose Aramaic would eventually replace Akkadian across the region.
evt-battle-halule: An Assyrian relief of King Sennacherib, who commanded the Assyrian army at Halule in 691 BCE — both sides claimed victory.
evt-nabopolassar: A foundation cylinder of Nabopolassar from Babylon — the Chaldean king who founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire by breaking Assyria's grip on the south.
evt-cre-birmingham-campaign: Birmingham, May 1963: young demonstrators huddle in a doorway as firefighters turn high-pressure hoses on them during the SCLC Birmingham campaign (Project C).
evt-xiongnu-battle-ikh-bayan: The Altai Mountains on the Mongolian steppe frontier — the region where the Han and Southern Xiongnu destroyed the Northern Xiongnu at the Battle of Ikh Bayan in 89 CE.
evt-genoese-caffa: The Genoese fortress towers at Caffa (modern Feodosia, Crimea), the Black Sea colony the Mongols besieged in 1346.
evt-knossos-palace: Map of Minoan Crete showing the palace at Knossos and the island other major centers.
evt-baekje-founding: A map of the Korean peninsula around 375 CE showing Baekje at its height, generations after the kingdom was founded.
evt-mi-shastri-pm: Lal Bahadur Shastri, who became prime minister of India in 1964 after Nehru death.
evt-asuka-baekje-fall: A map of the Korean peninsula around 375 CE showing the kingdom of Baekje, the Paekche ally whose fall in 660 drew Yamato Japan into war.
evt-sungkyunkwan: The Myeongnyundang lecture hall at Sungkyunkwan, the royal Confucian academy in Seoul.
evt-tumipampa-capital: The ruins of Pumapungo at Cuenca, Ecuador — the Inca city of Tumipampa, the empire northern capital.
evt-atahualpa-ransom: The Ransom Room (Cuarto del Rescate) at Cajamarca, where Atahualpa gold and silver ransom was gathered for Pizarro.
evt-venetian-trade-privileges: Southeastern Europe around 1000 — the Byzantine Balkans and Adriatic where Venice won its trade privileges.
evt-aksum-incense-trade: The Red Sea, the maritime artery of the Aksum incense and ivory trade.
evt-latin-american-independence-001: Charles III of Spain, the Bourbon king whose reforms tightened royal control over the colonies.
evt-latin-american-independence-119: A market scene in French Saint-Domingue, the Caribbean's richest sugar colony.
evt-latin-american-independence-028: Miguel Hidalgo, the priest whose rebel host was shattered at the Battle of Calderon Bridge.
evt-latin-american-independence-068: Agustin de Iturbide in imperial robes, crowned Emperor of the short-lived First Mexican Empire.
evt-latin-american-independence-072: King John VI acclaimed at Rio de Janeiro, now the seat of the Portuguese monarchy.
evt-latin-american-independence-031: A free man of color in revolutionary uniform, of the kind who filled both patriot and royalist armies.
evt-latin-american-independence-013: Toussaint Louverture, the general who led enslaved people to victory in the Haitian Revolution.
evt-latin-american-independence-018: The Portuguese royal family arrives in Brazil after fleeing Lisbon ahead of the French.
evt-latin-american-independence-073: King John VI of Portugal, who sailed home to Lisbon and left his son Pedro as regent in Brazil.
evt-latin-american-independence-026: Francisco de Miranda, leader of the short-lived First Venezuelan Republic.
evt-latin-american-independence-085: Jose Antonio Paez, the llanero hero who led Venezuela out of Gran Colombia and ruled it for decades.
evt-latin-american-independence-116: The death of Antonio Jose de Sucre, ambushed and shot in the mountains of southern Colombia.
evt-latin-american-independence-087: Jose de San Martin in old age, during his long, forgotten exile in Europe.
evt-latin-american-independence-075: Prince Pedro proclaims Brazil's independence at the Ipiranga brook, the Cry of Ipiranga.
evt-latin-american-independence-082: Simon Bolivar, who took dictatorial power in a bid to hold Gran Colombia together.
evt-latin-american-independence-086: Facundo Quiroga, an Argentine caudillo, the personalist strongman typical of the new republics.
evt-latin-american-independence-121: An engraving of the Tumult of Aranjuez, the mob seizing the minister Godoy and toppling Charles IV.
evt-latin-american-independence-024: The open cabildo of Buenos Aires during the May Revolution, deciding to remove the Spanish viceroy.
evt-latin-american-independence-056: The La Rotonda monument in Guayaquil, where San Martin and Bolivar met once behind closed doors.
evt-latin-american-independence-115: Priests bless the rebel banners of the 1817 Pernambucan Revolt against the crown in Rio.
evt-latin-american-independence-099: A naval clash of the War of the Pacific, the Esmeralda sinking at the Battle of Iquique.
evt-latin-american-independence-101: The handwritten Rio Branco Free Womb Law, freeing children born to enslaved mothers in Brazil.
evt-latin-american-independence-106: Cuban cavalry charging under Antonio Maceo in the last war for independence from Spain.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-005: A depiction of Africans seized in a raid to be sold into the slave trade — the violent capture at the trade’s African source, here at its earliest transatlantic reach to the Americas.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-006: A 16th-century Indigenous-drawn codex showing a Spanish encomendero assaulting an Indigenous laborer — a contemporary record of the violence of the encomienda system.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-010: Bartolomé de las Casas, the Dominican friar who argued at the Valladolid debate that Indigenous people were fully human and must not be enslaved.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-011: Frans Post's painting of a sugar mill (engenho) in Pernambuco, Brazil, with enslaved laborers in the foreground — the plantation economy that drove Brazil's sugar boom.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-018: Enslaved laborers cutting sugar cane on a Caribbean plantation, an overseer on horseback behind them — the brutal sugar economy that made islands like Barbados rich.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-031: A period watercolor of the slave ship Marie Séraphique, captives crowded along the deck — a vessel built to carry human beings as cargo.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-037: An early-19th-century view of the British slaving fort on Bunce Island in the Sierra Leone River, ships riding at anchor offshore.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-043: Enslaved laborers loading hogsheads of sugar for shipment on a Caribbean coast — the sugar wealth that made colonies like Saint-Domingue the richest on earth.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-058: The Battle of Vertières (1803), the decisive engagement of the Saint-Domingue revolution, in which the formerly enslaved army defeated the French.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-065: William Wilberforce, the parliamentary leader of the decades-long campaign that won Britain abolition of the slave trade in 1807.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-074: A contemporary 1831 woodcut of Nat Turner’s rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia — a sensational pro-slavery print made to stoke fear of revolt.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-076: The Wedgwood “Am I Not a Man and a Brother?” medallion, the emblem of the British abolition movement that pressed for the 1833 act ending slavery across most of the empire.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-095: The Memorial to the Abolition of Slavery in Nantes, the French port that outfitted more slave ships than any other.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-097: Marcus Garvey, the Pan-Africanist leader and founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association, in ceremonial dress in 1922.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-106: Agostino Brunias's painting of a West Indian market, depicting the mixed African and European Creole society of the colonial Caribbean.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-007: An engraving of the King of Kongo — the conventional period image of Afonso I, the Catholic ruler who protested the seizure of his free subjects.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-030: The Brookes diagram of a British slave ship, captives packed in rows below decks — the harrowing reality of the Middle Passage crossing.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-041: An 18th-century engraving of a slave revolt in Jamaica, taken to depict Tacky’s uprising of 1760–61.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-050: The Brookes broadside, showing enslaved Africans stowed in a slave ship — the abolition movement’s most widely reproduced image.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-060: A period print of the 1791 uprising in Saint-Domingue, the revolt that forced revolutionary France to abolish colonial slavery.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-062: The Battle of Palm Tree Hill in Saint-Domingue, where yellow fever and fierce resistance destroyed Napoleon’s expedition.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-075: Albert Duperly’s print of the burning of the Roehampton estate during the Baptist War, the 1831–32 Jamaica rebellion.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-081: Jean-Baptiste Debret's depiction of slavery in Brazil, an overseer with a whip — the institution Brazil kept long after halting the Atlantic trade.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-084: The manuscript of Brazil’s 1871 Law of the Free Womb (Lei do Ventre Livre), which declared children born to enslaved women free.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-089: A Gullah woman weaving a sweetgrass basket in Charleston, a craft carried from West and Central Africa to the Sea Islands.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-090: The Cecil Rhodes statue being removed from the University of Cape Town in 2015, part of a wider reckoning with the legacies of slavery and empire.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-091: A botanical illustration of sugar cane (Saccharum officinarum), the labor-hungry crop that drove the Atlantic trade.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-098: A reproduction of a 1769 Charleston handbill advertising the sale of enslaved Africans just landed from a slave ship — the trade reduced to commerce.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-103: A 1738 indenture certificate binding Henry Mayer to years of service — the indentured labor that preceded hereditary racial slavery in the English colonies.
evt-age-of-exploration-005: A full-size replica of the caravel La Pinta — the small, nimble lateen-rigged ship that opened up the Atlantic coast.
evt-age-of-exploration-013: A period portrait long identified as King John II of Portugal, the spymaster prince who ran the push toward India.
evt-age-of-exploration-019: Brass mariner's astrolabes in a museum case at Lagos, Portugal — the ring sailors used to read the sun's height and find their latitude.
evt-age-of-exploration-032: An anonymous portrait of Vasco da Gama, the captain who rounded Africa and reached India by sea, wearing the cross of the Order of Christ.
evt-age-of-exploration-035: A devotional-panel detail of King Manuel I of Portugal at prayer, the monarch who presided over Portugal’s golden age of exploration.
evt-age-of-exploration-068: The printed title page of the New Laws of 1542, the royal code that tried to curb the encomienda and ban indigenous slavery.
evt-age-of-exploration-078: A silver eight-reales coin of Ferdinand and Isabella — the Spanish dollar, or piece of eight, that became the early-modern world’s money.
evt-age-of-exploration-096: An engraving of a King of Kongo (Manikongo), the title held by the Christian ruler Afonso I, who begged Portugal to stop the slavers bleeding his kingdom.
evt-age-of-exploration-097: A hand-colored lithograph of Queen Njinga (Nzinga Mbande) of Ndongo and Matamba, who outmaneuvered the Portuguese in Angola for decades.
evt-age-of-exploration-106: Bleeding, scorbutic gums caused by vitamin-C deficiency — the classic sign of scurvy, the disease that killed more sailors than storms.
evt-age-of-exploration-119: A wooden cross-staff, the cheap star-sighting instrument a sailor slid along a crosspiece to read his latitude.
evt-age-of-exploration-142: A 1683 engraving of a Portuguese galleon, the big, heavily gunned ship that hauled the Atlantic treasure fleets and the Pacific run.
evt-age-of-exploration-026: A carved-stone Taíno zemi, a three-pointed religious object of the Caribbean people Columbus met across the Greater Antilles.
evt-age-of-exploration-028: A portrait of Pope Alexander VI, who issued the Inter caetera papal bulls handing Spain dominion over the lands Columbus had found.
evt-age-of-exploration-031: A page from the Codex Kingsborough showing a Spanish encomendero abusing an indigenous man — a contemporary protest against the encomienda.
evt-age-of-exploration-059: A mural of the meeting between the Spanish and the Tlaxcala, the indigenous nation whose warriors made the conquest of the Aztecs possible.
evt-age-of-exploration-069: A portrait of Fray Bartolomé de las Casas, who argued at the Valladolid debate that indigenous Americans were rational humans with rights.
evt-age-of-exploration-073: A portrait of Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Society of Jesus — the Jesuits, spearhead of Catholic missionary expansion.
evt-age-of-exploration-088: A painting of Samuel de Champlain arriving at Quebec, greeted by indigenous canoes — the founding moment of New France and its fur trade.
evt-age-of-exploration-094: Auguste Biard’s painting of captive Africans being branded and loaded onto a slave ship — the Atlantic slave trade at full industrial scale.
evt-age-of-exploration-103: The Toruń portrait of Nicolaus Copernicus, who published the claim that the Earth circles the sun.
evt-age-of-exploration-107: A field of growing tobacco plants — the American crop that became the cash plant that saved Virginia and the era’s first global craze.
evt-age-of-exploration-108: A circa-1590 painting of the Manila galleon met by Chamorro canoes in the Pacific — the ship that bridged the last ocean and linked the continents.
evt-age-of-exploration-121: The Fortaleza Ozama, the oldest surviving European fortress in the Americas, built at Santo Domingo on Hispaniola.
evt-age-of-exploration-130: A painting of the Spaniards’ first interview with Atahualpa’s people at Cajamarca, the meeting that turned into the ambush of the Inca emperor.
evt-age-of-exploration-131: The jungle-buried stone ruins of Espíritu Pampa, the site of Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Neo-Inca State.
evt-age-of-exploration-133: A Spanish colonial silver eight-reales coin struck at the Potosí mint — the New World silver the crown skimmed with its royal fifth.
evt-age-of-exploration-143: A 16th-century painting of the port of Seville, crammed with shipping — the single harbor where Spain’s escorted treasure fleets unloaded their silver.
evt-age-of-exploration-030: A diagram of the Columbian Exchange, tracing the crops, animals, and diseases that crossed between the Old World and the New.
evt-age-of-exploration-066: Potosí beneath the silver mountain of Cerro Rico — the mines the mita labor draft fed with conscripted Andean villagers.
evt-age-of-exploration-099: Ears of maize — the New World grain whose spread across the Old World was one of the great crop transfers of the Columbian Exchange.
evt-dido-founds-carthage: Dido illustrated in the Vergilius Vaticanus, a late-Roman illuminated manuscript of Virgil's Aeneid (c. 400 CE) — the kind of source through which the West remembers her.
evt-byrsa-hill: Excavated foundations of Punic houses on Byrsa hill, with a surviving storage jar and cisterns set among the courtyard walls.
evt-tophet-sanctuary: Carved votive stelae standing in the Tophet precinct at Carthage, the kind of markers that crowned the buried urns.
evt-baal-hammon-worship: Terracotta statue of Baal Hammon enthroned, bearded and flanked by winged sphinxes (Thinissut sanctuary, Bardo National Museum, Tunis).
evt-tanit-ascendancy: A Punic votive stele carved with the classic "sign of Tanit" — a triangle topped by a horizontal bar and a disc — the emblem of Carthage's chief goddess.
evt-melqart-cult-carthage: Stele showing the god Melqart, striding above a lion — the Phoenician patron deity of Tyre whose cult Carthage carried west.
evt-punic-script: Bilingual dedication at the theater of Leptis Magna, Libya — Latin above, Neo-Punic below — showing the script still in use under Roman rule.
evt-carthage-walls: Museum reconstruction painting of Carthage, showing the walled peninsula and the ringed military harbor that the great fortifications enclosed.
evt-carthage-early-trade: Carthaginian silver coin (tetradrachm) carrying the head of the goddess Tanit — struck from the silver wealth that flowed through Carthage's trade.
evt-carthage-sardinia: The seaside ruins of Tharros on Sardinia's west coast, one of the Phoenician-founded ports Carthage took over.
evt-carthage-shipbuilding: The reconstructed remains of the Punic warship recovered off Marsala, Sicily — the actual archaeological proof of Carthage's prefab shipbuilding.
evt-battle-himera-480: Giuseppe Sciuti's 19th-century painting of the rout at Himera, with Hamilcar's sacrificial fire blazing at left.
evt-aristotle-constitution: Marble bust of Aristotle (Roman copy after a Greek original), Palazzo Altemps, Rome.
evt-african-territorial-empire: The reach of Carthage's empire (English-labeled map), with the North African heartland anchoring its territory and colonies.
evt-gold-trade-west-africa: A Carthaginian gold stater (c. 350–320 BCE): the goddess Tanit wreathed in grain on one face, the Punic horse on the other.
evt-sacred-band-carthage: A gilded Carthaginian breastplate from Ksour es-Saf (Bardo Museum, Tunis) — the kind of splendid armor that marked out Carthage's aristocratic soldiers.
evt-agathocles-invasion: Gold coin of Agathocles of Syracuse: helmeted Athena on one side, a winged thunderbolt and griffin with his royal title on the other.
evt-cothon-harbor: Aerial view of the surviving circular Punic military harbor at Carthage, its central admiralty island still visible as a lagoon.
evt-kerkouane: A pink-plaster Punic bathtub still set in its house at Kerkouane — the kind of in-home bathing that surprised excavators.
evt-grain-exports: Excavated Punic-quarter ruins on Byrsa Hill at Carthage, with the city and the sea beyond — the metropolis that the African grain lands fed.
evt-first-punic-war-begins: A row of bronze Carthaginian and Roman warship rams, recovered from the waters off Sicily and shown together in a museum case — the surviving hardware of the long sea war that opened in 264 BCE.
evt-siege-agrigentum: The Temple of Concordia at Agrigento — surviving ruins of the rich Greek city Rome stormed and emptied in 261 BCE.
evt-battle-mylae: Bronze warship rams of the kind torn from captured Punic ships to decorate Rome's victory columns.
evt-battle-ecnomus: A recovered bronze ram, the business end of the warships that fought one of antiquity's largest sea battles.
evt-hamilcar-barca-sicily: A Punic gilded bronze cuirass — the kind of armor a Carthaginian commander's force carried into the field.
evt-battle-aegates-islands: A bronze warship ram raised from the seabed off the Aegates Islands, its socket cast with a relief of a winged Victory — one of the rams torn from the fleets sunk in the battle of 241 BCE.
evt-mercenary-war: A silver shekel struck by the rebels, its Greek legend ΛΙΒΥΩΝ proclaiming a breakaway "state of the Libyans."
evt-hamilcar-barca-spain: Benjamin West's painting of the legendary scene: Hamilcar holds young Hannibal at the altar to swear eternal enmity against Rome.
evt-hasdrubal-fair: A monument to Hasdrubal the Fair in Cartagena, the city he founded as the Barcid capital in Spain.
evt-new-carthage-silver: A Barcid silver quarter-shekel minted at Carthago Nova — a wreathed head on the front, a war elephant on the back, struck from the local mines.
evt-hannibal-takes-command: Hannibal Barca rendered as a battle-hardened commander, the Carthaginian general who took charge of the army in Spain at twenty-six.
evt-siege-saguntum: The hilltop fortress of Sagunto, Spain — the long acropolis where the besieged townspeople made their last stand.
evt-crossing-alps: Heinrich Leutemann's illustration of the army struggling over the Alps, war elephants and all.
evt-battle-trebia: Bust traditionally identified as Hannibal Barca, the Carthaginian general who won his first Italian victory at the Trebia.
evt-battle-trasimene: Lake Trasimene and the wooded hills along the northern shore, where Hannibal concealed his entire army for the ambush.
evt-battle-cannae: Memorial column overlooking the flat Apulian plain near Cannae where Hannibal encircled the Roman army.
evt-scipio-africanus: Bronze bust of Scipio Africanus, the Roman general who carried the war to North Africa.
evt-hannibal-exile: Marble bust traditionally identified as Hannibal Barca, who died in exile rather than fall into Roman hands.
evt-numidian-cavalry: Numidian bronze coin of King Masinissa: a royal portrait on one face, a galloping horse — the Numidians' famous mount — on the other.
evt-war-elephants: Terracotta statuette of a war elephant carrying a fighting tower and rider, from Pompeii.
evt-religious-syncretism: A terracotta incense-burner shaped as the head of Baal Hammon, the bearded chief god of Carthage, crowned with a feathered headdress.
evt-purple-dye-production: Shells of the spiny dye-murex, the Mediterranean sea snail whose mucus gland yielded Tyrian purple.
evt-carthage-coinage: A silver Carthaginian tetradrachm (c. 350-320 BCE) showing the head of the goddess Tanit, the signature Punic coin portrait.
evt-balearic-slingers: Ancient sling-stones of the kind hurled by Balearic slingers, shaped to fly straight and hit hard.
evt-terence-playwright: The medieval manuscript portrait of Terence (Vatican Library, Vat. lat. 3868), the standard image of the playwright.
evt-punic-inscriptions: A Punic votive stele carved with a cultic scene and an inscription in the Punic alphabet, the kind of stone that fills the tophets.
evt-cato-delenda-est: A gaunt, hard-faced Roman marble bust traditionally identified as Cato the Elder, carved in the unflattering 'veristic' style that prized every wrinkle as proof of character.
evt-third-punic-war-begins: A museum case of Third Punic War relics from the siege — a corroded iron sword, lead sling-bullets, and a heavy stone catapult ball, the everyday hardware of the final defense.
evt-destruction-carthage: The ruins of Carthage above the sea, a lone column still standing - all that the Romans left of the city they burned to the ground in 146 BCE and later rebuilt.
evt-punic-literature-lost: A Punic limestone stele incised with rows of the Carthaginian alphabet — votive and funerary stones like this are nearly all the written Punic that survives, since the literature itself is gone.
evt-carthage-economic-recovery: A Carthaginian silver double shekel of roughly 160–149 BCE: the goddess Tanit on the front, a horse on the back — coinage from the very decades the city's wealth alarmed Rome.
evt-temple-eshmun-carthage: The summit of the Byrsa hill at Carthage, scattered with column capitals and ruins beneath the old Acropolium — the high point of the city where the great temple of Eshmun once stood.
